gbs333-h54165-d1e102.summary: Rubric marking the beginning of the second question of the distinction.

gbs333-h54165-d1e111.summary: States the second question, which concerns the proper matter of the distinction more directly than the general question on virtue: whether one infused faith is sufficient and necessary for believing all credible truths.
concepts: sufficiency and necessity of infused faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e118.summary: Announces the three-article structure: notabilia clarifying terms, the conclusive response, and the resolution of doubts.

gbs333-h54165-d1e129.summary: Following Alexander of Hales (Summa III q. 74), lists eleven scriptural and theological senses of 'fides': a promise, fidelity, conscience, assent to a conclusion accepted on probable grounds, the knowledge of the homeland, the creed, the sacrament of faith (baptism, as with infants' faith in Augustine), unformed habit, formed habit, and the act of believing. Each is given a scriptural or patristic example.
claims: 'Fides' has many senses, including promise, fidelity, conscience, probable assent, creed, baptism, unformed and formed habit, and act of believing.

gbs333-h54165-d1e245.summary: Of these, three senses are most common: faith as act (assent to revealed truth), as habit (acquired from repeated assents or infused immediately by God, inclining the intellect to assent to revealed truths), and as object (the truth believed or the thing it signifies).
claims: Faith as act is assent to revealed truth.
Faith as habit is either acquired by repeated assents or infused by God, and inclines to assent to revealed truths.
Faith as object is the truth believed or what it signifies.
concepts: act, habit, and object of faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e278.summary: Gives scriptural examples of the three senses: Romans 10 ('faith comes from hearing') for the act, Hebrews 11 ('without faith it is impossible to please God') for the habit, and 1 Timothy 4 ('nourished in the words of faith', i.e. truths to be believed) for the object.
claims: Hebrews 11:6 is to be understood of habitual faith.
concepts: act, habit, and object of faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e319.summary: Each sense can be subdivided. Actual and habitual faith divide into formed and unformed, as Lombard, following Augustine, says that faith by which we believe is a virtue when formed by charity and not a virtue when without charity (then empty and dead). We believe formally by actual faith and by habitual faith as a disposition that co-causes and inclines to a firmer act of believing.
claims: Faith formed by charity is a virtue; unformed faith is not a virtue.
We believe formally by the act of faith; the habit is a co-cause inclining to firmer belief.

gbs333-h54165-d1e369.summary: Faith in these senses can also be divided into acquired and infused.
claims: Faith divides into acquired and infused.

gbs333-h54165-d1e378.summary: Faith in the third sense, as object, can be subdivided in many ways according to the different articles and truths to be believed.

gbs333-h54165-d1e391.summary: Notes that faith must be defined differently according to these different senses, which is why the saints and doctors define it in various ways.

gbs333-h54165-d1e403.summary: Lombard's definition: faith is the virtue by which what is not seen is believed. With Augustine, he restricts this to unseen things that pertain to religion.
claims: Faith is a virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed.

gbs333-h54165-d1e427.summary: Lombard's definition concerns formed habitual faith, as the term 'virtue' indicates.
claims: Lombard defines formed habitual faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e436.summary: Hugh of St. Victor's definition (De sacramentis I.10.1): faith is a certitude, that is, a certain cognition of the mind about absent things, placed above opinion and below science.
claims: Faith is a certain cognition of absent things, above opinion and below science.

gbs333-h54165-d1e469.summary: Explains 'certitude' in Hugh's definition as a certain adhesive cognition, which distinguishes faith from estimation, conjecture, and opinion, which coexist with doubt and fear of the opposite. Where there is still doubt there is no faith.
claims: Faith excludes doubt and fear of the opposite, unlike opinion and conjecture.

gbs333-h54165-d1e492.summary: Explains 'below science' as referring to cognition, not merit. If believing were not sometimes more than seeing, vision would not be withheld to make faith meritorious, nor would 'Blessed are those who have not seen and believed' have been said. But regarding happiness and perfection of truth, seeing the present is more than believing the absent. So the evidence of science is excluded: if you see, it is not faith.
claims: Faith is inferior to science in cognition but can exceed it in merit.
Faith excludes the evidence proper to science.

gbs333-h54165-d1e533.summary: Hugh's definition is general, fitting actual and habitual, infused and acquired faith, provided 'certitude' is extended to both actual and habitual cognition.
claims: Hugh's definition applies to all forms of faith, actual and habitual, infused and acquired.

gbs333-h54165-d1e547.summary: John Damascene's definitions (De fide orthodoxa IV), conforming to the Apostle: faith is the hypostasis (substance) of things hoped for, or faith is an unsought assent concerning the first truth.
claims: Faith is an assent, not reached by inquiry, to the first truth.

gbs333-h54165-d1e571.summary: Damascene's definition concerns faith's principal act, assent to the revealing first truth, which is 'unsought' because it is received by revelation, not reached by argumentative reasoning.
claims: The principal act of faith is assent to the first truth revealing.
Faith's assent is received by revelation, not acquired by argument.

gbs333-h54165-d1e587.summary: Dionysius's definition (De divinis nominibus I): faith is the simple reason of self-existent truth. 'Simple reason' means cognition received by revelation, not by argumentative inquiry, and 'self-existent truth' means the first or certain truth.
claims: Faith is knowledge of the first truth received by revelation, not by argument.

gbs333-h54165-d1e615.summary: Augustine's further description (to Consentius): faith is the illumination of the mind toward the highest truth, that is, revealed cognition illuminating the mind to know the highest truth.
claims: Faith is revealed cognition illuminating the mind toward the highest truth.

gbs333-h54165-d1e634.summary: Augustine's description concerns faith in its most perfect act of believing.

gbs333-h54165-d1e643.summary: Gives the Apostle's definition (Hebrews 11): faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the argument of things not apparent.
claims: Faith is the substance of things hoped for and the argument of things not apparent.

gbs333-h54165-d1e656.summary: Interprets the Apostle's definition. It defines formed faith, not faith in general. Since faith is a habit and habits are known by acts and objects, it is defined through its act and objects. The act of believing is the intellect's assent under the will's command (no one believes unless willing, says Augustine), so it has both the true (the intellect's object) and the good or end (the will's object). 'Argument' indicates the act; 'not apparent' the intellect's object, non-evident truth held firmly on divine authority; 'things to be hoped for' the will's object; and 'substance' the genus or quiddity. 'Substance' is taken connotatively, from substare, as a beginning (Aquinas II-II q. 4 a. 1; Nicholas of Lyra), or as a cause or foundation (the Gloss). Faith, as the first infused virtue without which no one attains the hoped-for goods (the vision and fruition of God), begins future beatitude and makes those goods exist now cognitively in believers and later really. 'Argument' means certitude, firm adherence to what does not appear.
claims: The Apostle defines formed faith, through its act and its objects.
The act of believing is the intellect's assent commanded by the will.
Faith holds non-evident truth firmly on divine authority, not on the evidence of the thing.
Faith is the substance of things hoped for as the beginning, cause, and foundation of future beatitude.
Faith is the first infused virtue, without which the hoped-for goods cannot be attained.

gbs333-h54165-d1e797.summary: Paraphrases the Apostle's definition accordingly: formed faith is a beginning, cause, or foundation of attaining the goods hoped for in beatitude, and a certain and firm adhesive cognition of what is hoped for and not yet apparent, since hope that is seen is not hope (Romans 8).
claims: Formed faith is the beginning of beatitude and a firm adhesive cognition of things not yet apparent.

gbs333-h54165-d1e823.summary: 'Substance of things to be hoped for' distinguishes formed faith from faith commonly taken, which also concerns things not ordered to beatitude ('I believe John is running'). It also distinguishes it from unformed faith, which, not being meritorious, is not a principle or cause of the things hoped for.
claims: Unformed faith is not meritorious and so is not the substance of things hoped for.

gbs333-h54165-d1e845.summary: 'Argument' distinguishes faith from opinion, suspicion, and doubt, which are held with fear of the opposite.
claims: Faith differs from opinion, suspicion, and doubt by lacking fear of the opposite.

gbs333-h54165-d1e856.summary: 'Not apparent' distinguishes faith from science and understanding, and generally from evident cognition. From these Aquinas gathers a formal definition: faith is a habit of the mind by which eternal life is begun in us, making the intellect assent to things not apparent. 'Firmly and certainly' must be added, or the definition would fit opinion. With 'adhesive cognition' instead of 'habit', it would cover both act and habit, and the Apostle's definition does not exclude the formed act, by which we merit. All the cited definitions are good and formal if rightly expounded, though not equally general.
claims: Faith differs from science and understanding by concerning the non-evident.
Aquinas's definition needs 'firmly and certainly' to exclude opinion.
The formed act of faith is meritorious.
All the cited definitions are sound if rightly interpreted, though of differing generality.

gbs333-h54165-d1e904.summary: Gathers a general definition of faith as it concerns theology, covering infused and acquired, habitual and actual, formed and unformed faith: faith is a certain and firm adhesive cognition of truth pertaining to religion, received by revelation.
claims: Faith in general is a certain and firm adhesive cognition of religious truth received by revelation.

gbs333-h54165-d1e934.summary: Explains 'adhesive cognition' as including both actual assent and the acquired or infused habit inclining to assent, since adhesive cognition is commonly divided into actual and habitual. 'Certain and firm' excludes adhesive cognitions held with fear of the opposite.
claims: 'Adhesive cognition' covers both the act and the habit of assent.

gbs333-h54165-d1e958.summary: Notes that although the doctors often use certitude, firmness, and evidence interchangeably, properly taken they differ considerably, and knowing the difference shows how faith is certain, firm, or evident compared with the other intellectual virtues.
claims: Certitude, firmness, and evidence differ when taken properly.

gbs333-h54165-d1e980.summary: Certitude concerns the infallibility of the object, the believed truth: what is infallible is certain, since no one assenting to it is deceived.
claims: Certitude is the infallibility of the object.

gbs333-h54165-d1e995.summary: Firmness concerns the intellect's adherence, by which it holds to the truth constantly and without fear.
claims: Firmness is the constancy of the intellect's adherence without fear.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1008.summary: Evidence concerns the mode of manifestation, by which truth is shown so that the intellect cannot dissent. This happens through experiential knowledge presupposing intuitive cognition of the terms, through a proposition known from its terms, or through demonstration from such principles. Such evidence belongs to science and the understanding of principles, not to faith, which concerns non-evident truths.
claims: Evidence is a manifestation of truth that compels assent.
Evidence arises from experience, self-evident propositions, or demonstration.
Faith lacks evidence.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1043.summary: Faith is certain, indeed more certain than any human cognition in this life, because it concerns what God, the first and infallible truth, has revealed (John 1:18; 2 Peter 1:21). Its certitude is not surpassed by humanly acquired science but surpasses it. Even the vision of the homeland is not more certain, since the same God who shows himself there revealed the truths of faith here, though the vision is more evident. Patristic texts that seem to rank the certitude of science above faith are to be read with 'certitude' extended to mean evidence.
claims: Faith is more certain than any humanly acquired knowledge, because it rests on God's infallible revelation.
The beatific vision is more evident but not more certain than faith.
Authorities preferring the certitude of science must be read as speaking of evidence.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1118.summary: First objection to the certitude of faith: faith concerns contingents as well as necessary truths (e.g. that Christ will come to judge). Contingents can change, since Christ could not come, so such articles could be false and are not infallible.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1138.summary: Second objection: a believer can be moved by doubt about the object of faith, so faith is not certain, since certitude excludes all doubt.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1149.summary: Third objection: falsehood can underlie hope and charity, which presuppose faith, so it can underlie faith too. One foreknown to damnation can hope for beatitude, and one can tend in charity to something under invincible error, which excuses from sin and does not expel charity.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1167.summary: Answers the first objection. The contingency of some articles no more diminishes faith's certitude than the necessity of others increases it, because certitude rests not on the necessity of the truth believed but on divine revelation, which cannot deceive. God can reveal a future only if he foreknows it, and his foreknowledge is infallible. It imposes no necessity, so things can be otherwise in the divided sense, but revelation can never deceive in the composed sense. So it is granted that faith concerns contingents and that these, considered absolutely, can change from true to false. Considered under divine revelation and foreknowledge, which is how they fall under faith, they cannot be false. Christ could absolutely fail to come to judgment, but 'Christ, revealed as coming to judgment, does not come' is impossible. So the inference 'an article can be false, therefore faith can deceive the believer' fails, because deceiving the believer requires both that the article be revealed and that it be false, which cannot hold together.
claims: The certitude of faith rests on divine revelation, not on the necessity of what is believed.
Divine foreknowledge is infallible yet imposes no necessity on things.
Contingent revealed truths can be false in the divided sense but not in the composed sense, given the revelation.
A believer can never be deceived by faith, since an article being revealed and being false are incompatible.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1280.summary: Answers the second objection briefly, deferring to the next distinction, which treats how faith is corrupted. Certitude does not necessarily remove every motion of doubt arising on the believer's side, but it removes every possibility of being deceived.
claims: The certitude of faith excludes the possibility of deception, not every motion of doubt in the believer.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1296.summary: Answers the third objection, granting that falsehood can underlie hope and charity but denying the inference. Faith is an intellectual virtue whose object is the true, so it wholly excludes falsehood. Hope and charity belong to the intellectual appetite, whose object is the good, and do not exclude error. One can act from charity under invincible error, e.g. taking another's property believing it one's own if not culpable for the error. Hope and charity presuppose faith, but their acts also depend on other, non-faith cognitions, where error can arise. For example, rendering the marital debt for God's command is an act of charity, but faith tells one the debt must be paid, not that this woman is one's wife.
claims: As an intellectual virtue aimed at truth, faith excludes falsehood entirely.
Hope and charity, as appetitive virtues aimed at the good, can coexist with invincible error.
Acts of charity require cognitions beyond faith, in which error may occur.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1365.summary: Explains 'firm' in the general definition: it excludes suspicion and opinion, which carry fear of the opposite.
claims: Firmness excludes suspicion and opinion from faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1376.summary: Firmness of adherence belongs to the essence of faith: one who doubts in faith is an unbeliever (Decretals, De haereticis c. 1) and so lacks faith. Hence the Athanasian Creed: unless one believes faithfully and firmly, one cannot be saved.
claims: One who doubts in faith is an unbeliever and lacks faith.
Firm belief is necessary for salvation.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1407.summary: Augustine (actually Fulgentius), De fide ad Petrum, begins each article with 'hold most firmly and do not doubt at all'. The superlative is apt, since a wayfarer should adhere to no truth more firmly than to the truths of faith.
claims: A wayfarer should adhere to the truths of faith more firmly than to any other truth.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1437.summary: The martyrs show this: faith made them cling to believed truth more than any science to its known object, since neither blandishments nor torments could induce them even to speak against the faith. This does not happen in the sciences, since, as Bonaventure says, it would be foolish to die for a geometrical conclusion.
claims: Faith produces firmer adherence than science, as the martyrs show.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1474.summary: Explains 'of truth pertaining to religion': not every adherence to a truth on a speaker's authority, even if certain, is called faith (Augustine, Enchiridion 8, 15). What neither belongs to nor conduces to attaining happiness does not pertain to religion, by which God is worshiped in this life in order to beatify in the next. When asking what to believe, one need not investigate nature like the physicists, and some things are better not known.
claims: Theological faith concerns only truths pertaining to religion, ordered to beatitude.
Not every belief on authority counts as faith in the theological sense.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1532.summary: Explains 'received by revelation': faith rests not on demonstrative proofs or experience, which produce evident cognition, but only on the authority of the one revealing. This distinguishes it from science, prudence, wisdom, and the beatific vision.
claims: Faith rests on the authority of the revealer, not on demonstration or experience.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1559.summary: Announces that acquired and infused faith differ in many ways.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1568.summary: First difference: acquired faith is a habit naturally acquired by repeated acts of believing, while infused faith is a habit created by God supernaturally and immediately in the soul. Infused faith is called a habit not in the sense defined in the previous question (generated by acts) but because it is a quality God produces in the soul, inclining mediately or immediately to the same acts as the acquired habit.
claims: Acquired faith is generated by repeated acts; infused faith is created immediately by God.
Infused faith is a habit only in an extended sense, as a God-produced quality inclining to acts.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1597.summary: Further differences. (2) Acquired faith inclines immediately to the act of believing, requiring only apprehension of the credible: believing a reporter truthful, one believes what is reported, and the act generates the habit. Infused faith never inclines to belief about any object without acquired faith or its act. A baptized child raised alone, without instruction, has infused faith regarding its proper object, 'everything revealed by God is true', but can elicit no act about it, barring a miracle of divine illumination, unless taught and believing by acquired faith. The same holds for every particular article. (3) Infused faith is one for all articles, but acquired faith is not (see conclusions 5–6). (4) Infused faith is destroyed by any error about any article, while acquired faith coexists with error about another article. Both incline to the act of believing.
claims: Acquired faith inclines immediately to belief, given apprehension of the credible.
Infused faith cannot produce any act of belief without acquired faith.
The proper object of infused faith is the proposition 'everything revealed by God is true'.
Infused faith is one for all articles; acquired faith is not.
Infused faith is lost by error about any article; acquired faith is not.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1699.summary: Regarding how the infused habit inclines to believe the articles, there are two positions, both probable, neither demonstrable.
claims: Neither account of how infused faith inclines to belief can be demonstrated.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1708.summary: First position: just as acquired faith believes the truthfulness of a witness and therefore the article asserted, the believer rests not on the evidence of the object but on the truthfulness of the witness, God. Taking 'God is truthful, so everything asserted by God is true' as a major premise, one deduces each article by subsumption ('this is asserted by God; therefore it is true'). This is why faith is knowledge 'in part' and 'in a mirror, in an enigma' (1 Cor. 13). Infused faith has as its proper, immediate object the proposition 'everything revealed by God is true in the sense in which it is revealed', which serves as premise for every article (e.g. God is triune, incarnate, suffered). The infused habit inclines mediately to every act regarding any article by virtue of that proposition.
claims: Faith rests on the truthfulness of God as witness, not on the evidence of the object.
Particular articles are believed by subsumption under 'everything revealed by God is true'.
On this view, infused faith inclines immediately to that general proposition and mediately to all articles.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1806.summary: Refines the first position. Infused faith with the intellect and apprehension is not a sufficient principle of belief; acquired faith about the same object is also required. Once acquired faith in 'everything revealed by God is true' is present, infused faith can concur immediately with it and the intellect as a partial cause of the first theological, and (if formed) meritorious, act of belief in that proposition. It could not do so before, because a necessary partial cause was lacking. For the particular articles, the infused habit is a mediate cause, a cause of a cause, inclining to them only through its own act, as the habit of a principle inclines to the conclusion through the act of knowing the principle.
claims: Infused faith requires acquired faith as a co-cause to produce any act of belief.
Infused faith is an immediate partial cause of belief in its proper object and a mediate cause regarding particular articles.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1881.summary: Objection to the first position: if infused faith bears on 'everything revealed by God is true' and inclines to the articles only through that, then no one would ever assent by infused faith to 'God is triune and one'. One assents to it because it is revealed, and then one must ask how one assents to 'that God is triune and one is revealed by God'.
concepts: assent to the fact of revelation

gbs333-h54165-d1e1916.summary: Continues the objection: if one believes that it is revealed because it is revealed that it is revealed, the question recurs, producing an infinite regress, so nothing would ever be firmly believed, just as a conclusion resolved into principles ad infinitum would never be known, and nothing can depend essentially on infinitely many causes.

gbs333-h54165-d1e1945.summary: Further objection: if one assents to 'it is revealed that God is triune' by acquired faith, then infused faith would depend on acquired faith for its being and firmness, and acquired faith would be more perfect, as an equivocal cause is more perfect than its effect. Reply: the antecedent is admitted but the consequence denied. One believes 'God is triune' because it is revealed, and believes that it is revealed because one believes the witness (an apostle, Scripture) to be truthful, which is believed by acquired faith. Since infused faith never assents without acquired faith, there is no regress. Infused faith does not depend on any creature for its being, since God alone infuses and conserves it, as in baptized infants, who have no acquired faith.
claims: The regress stops in acquired faith in the truthfulness of the human witnesses (apostles, Scripture).
Infused faith depends on no creature for its being, since God alone infuses and conserves it.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2008.summary: Nor does infused faith depend on acquired faith for its firmness. Infused faith adds something beyond the firmness acquired faith gives, so someone with both elicits a more intense and firmer act than someone with acquired faith alone. Infused faith requires acquired faith as a partial agent to produce its act, so the act depends on both habits, the power, and apprehension, which together with God make one total cause. There is a single act to which both faiths concur. Acquired faith can produce an act without infused faith but not as perfect, intense, and firm, and not a theological and meritorious act without formed faith. So acquired faith is not more perfect than infused faith, since it is not its cause.
claims: Infused faith adds firmness and intensity beyond what acquired faith gives.
Acquired and infused faith concur in one and the same act of belief as partial causes with God.
Acquired faith alone cannot produce a meritorious theological act.
Acquired faith is not more perfect than infused faith, since it does not cause it.
concepts: concurrence of acquired and infused faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e2080.summary: Second position (Ockham, Quodl. III q. 7): infused faith inclines immediately and equally to the acts of all articles, not to one through another, though always with acquired faith concurring. As the sun concurs immediately with lower causes in generating plants, animals, and mixtures, but not without them, so God infuses faith as a habit universal in its causality, inclining immediately to any article to which acquired faith inclines. Since acts about different articles differ in species, infused faith is their equivocal, not univocal, cause, like the sun.
claims: On Ockham's view, infused faith inclines immediately to belief in every article, with acquired faith concurring.
Infused faith is a universal, equivocal cause of specifically distinct acts of belief, like the sun.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2128.summary: Article 2, first conclusion: acquired faith is necessary for believing the articles. Proved by Romans 10 ('faith comes from hearing... how will they hear without a preacher?'), which cannot refer to infused faith, created immediately by God. Also proved by reason (Scotus, this distinction): to believe the articles one must believe the Church to be truthful, and this is believed by acquired faith. Augustine: 'I would not believe the Gospel unless I believed the Church', and he rejects the Gospel of the Nazarenes because the Church does not admit it. Just as one believes famous historians because their authors are deemed truthful, one believes the Gospel because the Church holds its writers truthful, and by hearing one acquires the habit of believing them.
claims: Acquired faith is necessary for believing the articles of faith.
Belief in Scripture depends on prior belief in the Church's approval of it.
Belief in the Church's truthfulness is held by acquired faith, as with credible historians.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2218.summary: Further proof: as shown above, no article can be believed without acquired faith, since infused faith does not incline to assent without it.
claims: No article can be believed without acquired faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2229.summary: Further proof: no one doubts God's truthfulness, which is naturally implanted in everyone, nor the Church's approval of the words and writings of truthful men, so one adheres firmly to them by acquired faith from hearing.
claims: That God is truthful is naturally known to all.
Firm adherence to Church-approved teaching is possible by acquired faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2247.summary: Second conclusion: it cannot be proved by natural reason that infused faith is necessary for believing the articles. Acquired faith suffices for believing all credibles. An unbaptized gentile or Jewish child raised among believers would have no infused faith (nor charity, which is infused with it), yet, trusting its instructors, it would believe everything a Christian believes.
claims: The necessity of infused faith cannot be proved by natural reason.
An unbaptized person instructed among Christians could believe everything Christians believe by acquired faith alone.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2288.summary: Further proof: each article can be believed by acquired faith alone, so all can, since believing them together involves no contradiction (truth agrees with truth). For any article, one can believe it while erring about another, unrelated article, and then one lacks infused faith (as will be shown), so one believes that article without infused faith.
claims: Each article, and so all articles, can be believed by acquired faith alone.
One who errs about any article lacks infused faith yet can still believe other articles.
concepts: error and loss of infused faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e2310.summary: Further: as one believes a historian by acquired faith because one trusts him, one can by acquired faith alone believe that the Church, made up of the gravest men who condemn every lie and shed their blood for the articles, is truthful and approves only truths. One can then believe all it approves, which includes all the articles. That this is possible without infused faith is clear, because an unbaptized person in mortal sin, who lacks infused faith, can believe it.
claims: One can believe all articles by acquired faith alone, through belief in the Church's truthfulness.
The unbaptized and those in mortal sin can believe the Church's teaching without infused faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2349.summary: A fortiori: if one can believe less truthful pagan historians by acquired faith, all the more truthful Christians of proven life.
claims: Christian witnesses of proven life are more credible than pagan historians.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2359.summary: Reply to the objection that infused faith, though not needed for the substance of the act, is needed for firmer adherence. Even if infused faith makes adherence firmer than acquired faith alone, this cannot be proved by natural reason. One firmly believes without fear of the opposite that the world existed before oneself and that unseen cities exist (Greece, Constantinople, Jerusalem, Alexandria) because one does not doubt the narrators. Much less can one doubt the truthfulness of preachers of the faith confirmed by miracles and signs, so one can firmly believe their preaching by acquired faith.
claims: That infused faith gives firmer adherence cannot be proved by natural reason.
Acquired faith can be firm without fear of the opposite, as with belief in unseen cities.
Preachers confirmed by miracles are even more credible than ordinary narrators.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2409.summary: Further: heretics adhere firmly to error and die for it without any infused gift, so all the more can one adhere firmly to truth without infused faith.
claims: Firm adherence, even to the point of death, is possible without infused faith, as heretics show.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2422.summary: Third conclusion: that infused faith exists beyond acquired faith is believed and expressed in Scripture. Hebrews 11: without faith it is impossible to please God, yet many pleased God without acquired faith, such as the Holy Innocents killed by Herod and baptized infants, so they had infused faith. The Decretals (c. Maiores, De baptismo) and the Clementines (I, De summa trinitate) speak of the infusion of virtues (cf. Panormitanus), and 1 Corinthians 13 lists faith with the infused habits of hope and charity.
claims: The existence of infused faith is a matter of belief grounded in Scripture and Church teaching.
Infants who please God without acquired faith must have infused faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2464.summary: More scriptural proofs: the just live by faith (Romans 1), and by faith we are justified and made sons of God (Romans 3). This cannot mean acquired faith, which even demons can have. Ephesians 2: saved by grace through faith, and this not from yourselves but the gift of God, which cannot refer to acquired faith, our own work. A sign: two people hear the same preacher and see the same miracles, and one believes and the other does not, as with Christ and the apostles, because one receives the gift of faith from above. A persuasion (not a demonstration): God's law perfects completely, healing the soul as the body. Since the image of God in the soul's three powers was deformed by sin, Christ perfects the intellect by faith as he perfects the will by charity. This is not evident, since infused charity itself is only believed (I d. 17).
claims: Justifying faith cannot be acquired faith, which demons also have.
The different responses of hearers to the same preaching are a sign of infused faith as a gift.
That Christ perfects the intellect by infused faith as the will by charity is a persuasion, not a demonstration.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2545.summary: Fourth conclusion: for everything infused faith concerns, there can also be acquired faith. This follows because infused faith cannot incline to any act without acquired faith, and otherwise it would be in vain, since both faiths exist to incline to acts.
claims: Acquired faith can exist regarding every object of infused faith.
concepts: coextension of acquired and infused faith

gbs333-h54165-d1e2569.summary: Fifth conclusion: there are diverse acquired faiths for diverse articles, distinct not only in number but in species. Habits are distinguished by their acts (Ockham), and acts of believing different articles differ in species. Two acts of believing the same article (in John and Peter, or successively in one person) differ numerically. Acts of believing different, non-synonymous articles differ more than that, and since there is no mean between numerical and specific difference, they differ in species.
claims: Acquired faith in different articles consists of specifically distinct habits.
Habits are distinguished as their acts are.
Acts of believing different non-synonymous articles differ in species.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2625.summary: Further proof: things are specifically distinct when one is compatible with a contrary that the other is not (sweetness is compatible with whiteness, blackness is not). Items of the same kind share compatibilities and incompatibilities. Error is incompatible with acquired faith about the same article but not with acquired faith about another, as an Arian can believe Christ born of a virgin while erring about the Trinity. So acquired faiths in different articles differ in species.
claims: Things compatible and incompatible with different items are specifically distinct.
Error about one article is compatible with acquired faith in another, as with the Arians.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2697.summary: Sixth conclusion: there is one infused faith, inclining mediately or immediately to all articles. On the first position it inclines immediately to its proper object and mediately to the rest, and on the second immediately to all. It is the same in species in all believers, having the same kinds of objects and acts, and numerically one in each believer for all credibles. One person cannot have several infused faiths at once, though one can have them successively: if the first is destroyed by error and infused again after correction, the second is not numerically the same, since what is corrupted does not return the same in number, barring a special miracle.
claims: Infused faith is one habit for all articles.
Infused faith is specifically the same in all believers and numerically one in each.
Infused faith lost through error and restored is a numerically new habit.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2769.summary: Article 3, first doubt: what is infused faith for, if acquired faith already gives firm assent without fear of the opposite? Answer: since it is God's gift, it is surely given fruitfully, as nothing vain proceeds from divine goodness, even if its use is hidden from us. In first act, it perfects the intellect, being more perfect than acquired faith and than any naturally acquired habit (science, wisdom, prudence). Though acquired habits exceed it in evidence, as a supernatural habit causable only by God it is simply more perfect, a supernatural adornment of the soul. In second act, with acquired faith and the power it causes a more perfect act of belief in substance, intensity, and firmness. Hence the prayer 'Lord, increase our faith' and the collect for an increase of faith, hope, and charity, which comes through infused faith.
claims: God's gift of infused faith cannot be useless, even if its utility is hidden.
Infused faith is simply more perfect than any acquired habit, though less evident.
Infused faith makes the act of belief more perfect in substance, intensity, and firmness.
Prayer for increase of faith is answered through infused faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2880.summary: Second doubt: how is faith corrupted? Acquired faith is corrupted as habits generally are (see the previous question). Its act is corrupted by a contrary error about the same article, since one cannot believe and disbelieve the same article, though belief in one article coexists with error about another. The habit is corrupted by a contrary habit of error, or by long neglect, through lack of conservation, but not by an act of error about the same object, since acts are contrary to acts, not to habits. An act opposes a habit only mediately, by generating a contrary habit. So the act of faith can coexist with the habit of science or of error about the same object, and the habit of faith with acts of science, clear vision, or error.
claims: The act of acquired faith is destroyed by contrary error about the same article.
The habit of acquired faith is destroyed by a contrary habit or by long neglect, not by a single contrary act.
No act is directly contrary to a habit.

gbs333-h54165-d1e2945.summary: Proves the first point. Someone with the habit of science of a conclusion who forgets the demonstration while keeping the habit can later assent to it on a teacher's authority or because he believes it was once demonstrated to him. Likewise, someone who believes something he previously erred about still has the habit of error, feeling inclined toward the error until a habit of faith generated by belief corrupts it.
claims: An act of faith can coexist with a habit of science or of error about the same object.
concepts: coexistence of act and contrary habit

gbs333-h54165-d1e2978.summary: Proves the second point. Someone with a demonstrated science can forget the demonstration and be deceived by a false syllogism into dissenting, while still feeling inclined toward the science, and a temperate person can act intemperately. So the habit of faith can coexist with acts of science and clear vision. A habit coexists with the act of a contrary habit, but habits of contrary acts do not coexist: when acts are incompossible, so are their habits, and conversely (said probably). The act of faith is incompossible with the act of science and of clear vision about the same object, because faith essentially involves obscurity or non-evidence, while vision and science involve evidence and clarity.
claims: The habit of faith can coexist with acts of science and clear vision about the same object.
Habits of contrary acts cannot coexist.
The act of faith is incompatible with an act of science or vision about the same object, since faith requires obscurity.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3066.summary: Infused faith, infused by God alone through creation, is corrupted by God alone through annihilation, and no created cause can destroy it. It is lost demeritoriously, not through every mortal sin as charity is, but through pertinacious error about any article: one who errs deserves to lose the gift that inclines to assent to every article. So every heresy destroys infused faith, otherwise the same person would be both faithful and heretic. The same holds for pertinacious doubt, since one who pertinaciously doubts an article is a heretic, and no heretic has infused faith.
claims: Infused faith is destroyed only by God, by annihilation.
Infused faith is lost by pertinacious error or doubt about any article, not by every mortal sin.
No heretic has infused faith.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3116.summary: Stresses 'pertinaciously'. Non-pertinacious error or doubt about a particular article does not destroy infused faith, though it is incompatible with acquired faith about that article. One may explicitly err about or doubt a truth in the biblical canon while implicitly believing it. A layman who firmly believes the Catholic faith and everything in the Bible, but does not know that Sarah was Abraham's wife, or thinks she was his mother, or doubts it while ready to be taught, is not an unbeliever. He implicitly believes it by believing all of Scripture true.
claims: Non-pertinacious error or doubt does not destroy infused faith.
One can explicitly err about a scriptural truth while implicitly believing it through believing all Scripture true.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3164.summary: Refers the questions of which truths are Catholic and who is to be judged faithful, unbeliever, or heretic to Ockham's Dialogus, part 1, books 2–3.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3177.summary: It follows that infused and acquired faith differ in species, since pertinacious error about a particular object is incompatible with infused faith but compatible with acquired faith. It is not unfitting for two habits of different kinds to incline immediately to the same act in the same power, provided one is supernatural and the other acquired, though it would be unfitting if both were acquired.
claims: Infused and acquired faith differ in species.
Two specifically distinct habits can incline to the same act in one power if one is supernatural.
concepts: specific distinction of infused and acquired faith
plurality of habits for one act

gbs333-h54165-d1e3203.summary: Third doubt: whether unformed faith is a gift of God and a virtue. God's gifts are natural or gratuitous, and gratuitous gifts are either freely given (gratis data) or making pleasing (gratum faciens), as in 1 Corinthians 12 (cf. II d. 16). Taking 'gift' as gratuitous, acquired unformed faith is not a gift of God, since it is acquired by man's natural power under God's general influence, like an art or science, while a gratuitous gift exceeds nature's capacity and is added by God alone.
claims: Acquired unformed faith is not a gratuitous gift, being acquired by natural power.
A gratuitous gift exceeds the capacity of nature and is added by God alone.
concepts: gratia gratis data and gratum faciens

gbs333-h54165-d1e3260.summary: Infused unformed faith is a gift of God, since it is a habit supernaturally infused by God.
claims: Infused unformed faith is a gift of God.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3270.summary: For the second part of the doubt, following Alexander of Hales (III q. 74 m. 3), distinguishes four senses of 'virtue': (1) most commonly, divided into natural, political, and gratuitous; (2) commonly, divided into political (acquired) and gratuitous (infused); (3) strictly, only an infused habit, whether gratis datum or gratum faciens; (4) most strictly, a gratuitous habit making pleasing and directive of action. Only charity, or a habit formed by charity, is virtue in the fourth sense. This is Lombard's sense at the beginning of the distinction, where, following Augustine, he distinguishes faith by which one believes that is a virtue, faith by which one believes that is not a virtue, and what is believed.
claims: 'Virtue' has four senses, from natural dispositions to the gratuitous habit that makes pleasing.
In the strictest sense only charity, or habits formed by charity, are virtues.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3318.summary: Infused unformed faith is a virtue in the first three senses, as an infused, gratis datum habit, while formed faith is a virtue in the fourth. Acquired faith is a virtue in the first two senses, taking virtue as any acquired habit directing a power to some rectitude of its act, as intellectual habits are called virtues.
claims: Infused unformed faith is a virtue in senses 1–3; formed faith also in sense 4.
Acquired faith is a virtue in senses 1–2.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3342.summary: Fourth doubt: is acquired faith an intellectual or a moral virtue? Taken most commonly, virtue is a disposition perfecting a power to operate well (Ethics II, c. 6, with the examples of the eye and the horse). A good operation is one suited to the power's proper end. Since the intellect's end is knowing the true and the will's is attaining the good, a habit inclining the intellect to apprehend clearly and to assent promptly and firmly is an intellectual virtue, and one inclining the will to will good and nill evil with delight is a virtue of the will.
claims: Virtue in general is a quality perfecting a power for its proper end.
The intellect's virtue concerns knowing truth; the will's concerns attaining good.
concepts: virtue of the eye and horse

gbs333-h54165-d1e3416.summary: When virtue is divided into intellectual and moral, it is taken in the second sense, as political or gratuitous virtue, which some call human virtue since it belongs to man as rational. This excludes natural virtues of the eye, the horse, and irrational things. Intellectual virtue is a habit caused by apprehensive or adhesive acts of the intellect, inclining it to cognition of the object or adherence to truth.
claims: The intellectual/moral division concerns human (political or gratuitous) virtue only.
Intellectual virtue is a habit caused by acts of the intellect, inclining to cognition or assent.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3451.summary: Distinguishes senses of moral virtue. Most broadly, from mos as custom, any habit left by repeated acts, in which case all acquired virtue is moral, but this is too broad. More properly, it is virtue caused by acts of will that makes one praiseworthy. Since acts of will are either elicited (willing and nilling) or commanded (acts of any power under the will's command), moral virtue is taken most strictly for virtue from elicited acts of will, which is intrinsic virtue, and more broadly for virtue from elicited or commanded acts. The latter inheres in the intellect, sense, or executive power, wherever its acts are, and is moral only contingently, by extrinsic denomination.
claims: Moral virtue strictly is a habit from elicited acts of will and is intrinsically virtuous.
Moral virtue broadly includes habits from commanded acts, residing in other powers and virtuous only extrinsically.
Every habit inheres in the power where the acts causing it are.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3527.summary: Answer, first: taking moral virtue strictly, as moral by essence, no intellectual virtue is moral, because acts of intellect (cognition) and of will (willing and nilling) really differ and are not predicated of each other, and habits differ as their acts do.
claims: No intellectual virtue is a moral virtue in the strict sense.
concepts: real distinction of intellect and will acts

gbs333-h54165-d1e3561.summary: Second: taking moral virtue broadly, some intellectual virtues are moral, since the will can command the intellect to speculate, reason, and inquire, and habits inclining to such acts are both intellectual and moral. This holds only for some intellectual acts. Assent to evident truth and dissent from evident falsehood are not subject to the will's command: the intellect cannot fail to assent to an apprehended evident truth, whatever the will wants, except that the will can turn the intellect away from considering it. This is not so with non-evident truth.
claims: Some intellectual virtues are moral in the broad sense, as habits of acts the will commands.
Assent to evident truth is not subject to the will, except as to continued consideration.
Assent to non-evident truth can be subject to the will.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3637.summary: Third: all acquired faith is an intellectual virtue, being caused by elicited acts of the intellect, namely assent to a certain truth on a witness's authority.
claims: Acquired faith is an intellectual virtue.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3650.summary: Fourth: all acquired faith is a moral virtue in the second (broad) sense, since it is acquired from acts commanded by the will. When a certain but non-evident truth, not sufficiently proved, is apprehended, the intellect is not compelled to assent and can withhold assent, so if it assents firmly it does so willingly, by the will's command. As Augustine says, other things a person can do unwillingly, but he can believe only willingly.
claims: Acquired faith is a moral virtue in the broad sense, because assent to non-evident truth is commanded by the will.
No one believes except willingly.
concepts: Augustine: credere non potest nisi volens

gbs333-h54165-d1e3681.summary: Fifth: infused faith is properly neither moral nor intellectual but gratuitous virtue, since Aristotle's division concerns acquired virtues, not infused ones.
claims: Infused faith is a gratuitous virtue, outside Aristotle's moral/intellectual division.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3694.summary: Last doubt: are formed and unformed faith numerically the same or different habits, and likewise their acts? The same faith cannot be both formed and unformed at once, but faith that was unformed can be formed while remaining the same in substance, and conversely, and likewise the act. Charity is called the form of the virtues not because it inheres in them and gives them species, as substantial form does, but because through charity their acts are referred to the ultimate end, God loved for his own sake, which is their highest perfection. Unformed faith is simply faith not accompanied by charity in the same soul, and formed faith is faith accompanied by it. The habit is no more changed by charity's arrival or departure than a body by clothing, so the same habit and act of faith, infused or acquired, can be successively formed and unformed.
claims: The same habit of faith can be successively unformed and formed.
Charity is the form of the virtues by referring their acts to God as ultimate end, not by inhering in them.
Formed faith is faith accompanied by charity in the same soul; the habit itself is unchanged by charity's presence.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues

gbs333-h54165-d1e3792.summary: Objection: the end is the principal object of act and habit (previous question), so if charity refers faith to a new end, its object, act, and habit change and the prior habit is corrupted, since two infused or two acquired faiths about the same credible cannot coexist. Reply: the end is the principal object only of intrinsically virtuous acts and habits, i.e. the will's elicited acts. Acts and habits of faith inhere in the intellect and are virtuous only by extrinsic denomination, as commanded by the will. For them, the end is a circumstance, not an object, so they can remain the same when the end changes.
claims: The end is an object only for the will's elicited acts; for intellectual acts like faith it is a circumstance.
Acts and habits of faith can remain the same when the end to which they are referred changes.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3854.summary: Objection: at least moral virtues cannot be the same formed and unformed, since they and their acts are in the will. Reply: with charity, a new act is elicited, and if repeated it generates a new habit specifically distinct from the prior moral habit. For example, John has moral fortitude to face dangers for the common good (keeping peace, freeing his country from robbers). With charity, he wills to face dangers because of the divine precept to free his neighbor from harm, which is a specifically distinct act, and if repeated it generates a new habit. The prior unformed habit is not corrupted, because the new habit is not contrary to it, though they incline to different acts.
claims: With charity, acquired moral virtues give rise to specifically new acts and habits ordered to God.
The new charity-informed habit does not corrupt the prior moral habit, since they are not contraries.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3911.summary: As for acts, if the will cannot hold several acts at once, the prior act gives way when the second arrives, not because of contrariety but because the power cannot hold several at once, while the prior habit remains. This applies to acquired habits.
claims: If the will cannot hold two acts at once, the first yields to the second without contrariety, while its habit remains.
concepts: capacity of the will for simultaneous acts

gbs333-h54165-d1e3929.summary: For infused habits, no new habit is infused when charity arrives if one already existed; the pre-existing one is formed, as was said of faith.
claims: When charity arrives, pre-existing infused habits are formed rather than replaced.

gbs333-h54165-d1e3940.summary: Asks by which faith demons believe and tremble (James 2:19). They believe by actual faith based on signs, conjectures, and the Scripture they know, and from these acts a habit is generated in them. They do not have infused faith: they did not have it before the fall (as some hold), and it is not likely that God would give the gratuitous gift of unformed faith to those obstinate in malice and hatred of God after the fall. Closes the question.
claims: Demons believe by acquired faith from signs, conjectures, and Scripture.
Demons lack infused faith.

gbs333-h54165.summary: Quaestio 2 of III d. 23 turns from virtue in general to faith itself and asks whether one infused faith is sufficient and necessary for believing all credibles. Article 1 clarifies terms. Following Alexander of Hales, 'faith' has many senses, chiefly act (assent to revealed truth), habit (acquired or infused), and object. Biel reviews and reconciles the definitions of Lombard, Hugh of St. Victor, Damascene, Dionysius, Augustine, Hebrews 11 (expounded through its act and objects, with 'substance' as the beginning of beatitude), and Aquinas. He offers a general definition: faith is a certain and firm adhesive cognition of truth pertaining to religion, received by revelation. He distinguishes certitude (infallibility of the object), firmness (constancy of adherence), and evidence (compelling manifestation). Faith is maximally certain and firm but not evident. Its certitude holds even for contingent articles because revelation cannot deceive in the composed sense. Acquired faith arises from repeated acts. Infused faith is created by God, is one for all articles, and is lost by any pertinacious error. It cannot produce any act without acquired faith. On whether it inclines through 'everything revealed by God is true' or immediately to all articles (Ockham), both views are probable. Article 2 gives six conclusions. (1) Acquired faith is necessary, since faith comes from hearing and belief in Scripture rests on belief in the Church. (2) Natural reason cannot prove infused faith necessary, since acquired faith suffices for believing all articles firmly. (3) Infused faith is nonetheless taught by Scripture and the Church (infants, justification, faith as gift). (4) Acquired faith can extend to all the objects of infused faith. (5) Acquired faiths in different articles differ in species. (6) Infused faith is one. Article 3 resolves doubts. Infused faith perfects the intellect and makes belief more intense and firm. Acquired faith is corrupted by contrary habits or neglect, infused faith only by God upon pertinacious error or doubt, though implicit faith survives non-pertinacious error. Acquired and infused faith differ in species. Acquired unformed faith is not a gratuitous gift, but infused unformed faith is. Acquired faith is both intellectual and (broadly) moral, since belief is willed, while infused faith is gratuitous. The same habit of faith can be successively formed and unformed, because charity forms by referring acts to God, not by inhering. Demons have only acquired faith.
claims: Faith in general is a certain and firm adhesive cognition of religious truth received by revelation.
Faith is the most certain cognition in this life, though not evident.
Contingent articles of faith are infallible in the composed sense, given divine revelation and foreknowledge.
Acquired faith is necessary for believing any article, and belief in Scripture rests on belief in the Church.
Natural reason cannot prove the necessity of infused faith, since acquired faith can suffice for firm belief in all articles.
Infused faith exists as a matter of faith, attested by Scripture and the Church.
Infused faith cannot elicit any act without acquired faith, but it makes the act more perfect, intense, and firm.
Acquired faiths in different articles differ in species, while infused faith is one for all articles.
Infused faith is destroyed only by God, upon pertinacious error or doubt about any article.
Acquired and infused faith differ in species.
Acquired faith is an intellectual virtue and, because belief is willed, a moral virtue in the broad sense.
Charity forms faith by referring its acts to God, so the same habit of faith can be successively formed and unformed.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues
